title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork

reading.body:
A smart ring manufacturer is sued for claims that its AI-based sleep stage detection is unreliable, performing no better than random guessing. The device costs $300 and up, and the manufacturer markets it with a 95 percent accuracy claim compared to clinical sleep labs. The system was deployed to consumers without the complex equipment, such as electrodes to measure brain activity, that clinical sleep staging requires.

The manufacturer denies the allegations and states its rings measure multiple signals including heart rate and body temperature, validated in peer-reviewed studies. The manufacturer also notes its rings are not marketed as medical devices. Whether the claimed accuracy of the AI system has actually been validated under real-world use conditions, or whether validation studies match the marketing claims, is not established by the reporting.

reports.title: Oura, Smart Ring Maker, Sued for Alleged False Claims and Unreliable AI
Oura faces lawsuit accusing it of misleading consumers about sleep-tracking accuracy

summary:
Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, is facing a proposed class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco. The lawsuit alleges that Oura made false advertising claims about its sleep-tracking capabilities, specifically claiming the rings can accurately measure different sleep stages through AI technology. The suit contends that Oura's rings, priced at $300 and up, cannot detect the physiological signals necessary for accurate sleep measurement and instead rely on unreliable AI guesses comparable to random chance. The company markets its rings as having 95 percent sleep staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs, but the lawsuit argues that actual sleep labs require complex equipment including multiple electrodes to measure brain activity that Oura rings lack.

Oura denies the allegations, stating it stands behind its science and accuracy claims, noting that its rings measure multiple signals including heart rate and body temperature. The company emphasizes that while its rings are not medical devices and cannot replace clinical sleep studies, its sleep staging has been validated in multiple peer-reviewed studies. The lawsuit seeks class-action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear whether customers can join or what compensation they might receive if the case proceeds. This is not Oura's first legal challenge, as the company faces another ongoing class action involving alleged collection of personal information without customer consent.
